entries.title: Mongolian at a glance
body: Mongolian is spoken by about 3 million people in Mongolia and by several million more in Inner Mongolia, China. The standard language of Mongolia is based on the Khalkha dialect.
The verb comes last, and grammar is carried by endings added one after another to a word. Vowel harmony decides which form of an ending is used. There is no grammatical gender and no word for “the”.

entries.title: Two scripts
body: The traditional Mongolian script (ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ, mongol bichig) was adapted from the Old Uyghur alphabet in the 13th century. It is written in vertical columns from top to bottom, and the columns run from left to right. Letters join along a central spine and change shape at the start, middle and end of a word.

In Mongolia, Cyrillic has been the everyday script since the 1940s, with two extra letters, Ө and Ү. The traditional script is still taught in schools there, and is the main script in Inner Mongolia. Traditional spelling is older than the pronunciation, so a word can look quite different in the two scripts.

entries.title: Vowel harmony
entries.body: A word's vowels are either all “back” or all “front” (и goes with both). Endings come in matching forms, and о-words take о-endings, ө-words ө-endings.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: Before a noun, many numbers take a short attributive form: гурав (three) becomes гурван, as in гурван ном, three books.

examples.e: Are your animals fat and well? (a countryside greeting)

entries.title: Naadam
body: Naadam (Наадам) is Mongolia's biggest festival, held every July. It is built around the “three games of men”: wrestling, horse racing and archery, though women and girls now take part in archery and racing.
The horse races run across open country for 15 to 30 kilometres, and the riders are children.
